study.title: Revelation 20 - Satan, the saints and the final judgment
study.overview: This chapter subsequently presents the provisional limitation of Satan, the reign of the saints with Christ, the final defeat of evil, and universal judgment before the great white throne. The text emphasizes that the power of evil is real, but never sovereign: it is restrained by God, it fails against the saints, is finally condemned and, finally, all human beings are assessed before God. The chapter ends with the solemn claim that only those inscribed in the book of life escape from the lake of fire.

outline.title: Satan is imprisoned for a certain period
outline.explanation: John sees an angel descending from heaven with authority over the abyss and a chain to arrest the dragon, the old serpent, that is, the devil and Satan. The prison is real, but temporary: it prevents him from continuing to deceive the nations until the thousand years are completed. The detail of the seal reinforces the idea of limitation imposed by God, not of casual defeat.

outline.title: The Saints reign with Christ and evil receives their final sentence
outline.explanation: John sees thrones and persons who receive authority to judge; he also sees the martyrs and the faithful who have not submitted themselves to the beast or to their mark. They participate in the first resurrection, are declared blessed and holy, and reign with Christ as priests. After the established period, Satan is released, deceives the nations, gathers a final rebellion and is destroyed with fire coming from God; then it is cast into the lake of fire, where the beast and the false prophet were already.

outline.title: The Great White Throne and the fate of the dead
outline.explanation: The scene of the final judgment arises: the Judge sits on the great white throne, and the creation flees from his presence. The dead, large and small, are judged according to the works recorded in the books, and the book of life appears as a decisive reference. The sea, death, and Xeol deliver the dead, death and Xeol are thrown into the lake of fire, and at last all of whom is not in the book of life is cast into the same destiny.

study.context: The notes received present this chapter as one of the most difficult parts of the prophecy of Revelation. Matthew Henry notes that he might not have yet been fulfilled in the time of his commentary, and therefore recommends caution, avoiding excessively specific claims. Tyndale organizes the chapter in three blocks: the arrest of Satan, the reign of God's people, and the final deliverance of Satan for his last attempt to war. Adam Clarke also reads the passage as a sequence of defeat, reign, final release, judgment, and condemnation. The immediate background of the book itself already includes the defeat of the beast and the false prophet in the previous chapter, which prepares the scene of the final judgment.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that evil has limits set by God. Satan does not act freely or autonomously; his action is restrained, his last rebellion is brief and his destiny is final. The text also values the persevering fidelity of the saints, especially those who suffered because of Jesus: they are vindicated, participate in the first resurrection and reign with Christ. The first expression resurrection is understood in the notes as the participation of the faithful in life and honor before God, in contrast to the second death, which represents eternal punishment. The final judgment shows the righteousness of God: no one escapes divine evaluation, and eternal life is not treated as a human right, but as a grace granted to those who belong to the book of life. At the same time, the text holds strict justice against sin and hope for the faithful, who are called priests of God and Christ.

scholarViews.insight: Satan's prison is presented as a preliminary and limited defeat, showing that the power of evil is restricted by God and that the faithful will not be deceived as long as this limitation lasts.

The chapter should be read with prudence, because its prophetic details are difficult; yet, the final judgment is certain and described as the great day in which everyone attends before the court of Christ.
The book of life functions as a decisive criterion in the judgment: whoever is not found in it is cast into the lake of fire, an image of the final destiny of the enemies of God and the apostates.

questions: What practical difference makes known that Satan is limited by God and not sovereign over history?
How should the promise that the faithful will reign with Christ should strengthen perseverance in the midst of pressure and persecution?
What changes in the way of living when it takes itself seriously that everyone will appear before the great white throne?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to the fear of God and to persevering faithfulness. Examine whether your hope is in justice itself, in the recorded works, or in actually belonging to the book of life. In times of pressure, reject any form of commitment to evil that seems advantageous in the short term. Keep firm in the testimony of Jesus, remembering that the final victory belongs to Christ and that injustice, death and deception will not have the final word.
study.uncertainty: The given notes do not resolve whether the millennium should be understood more literally or symbolically, nor do they detail the exact relationship between the first resurrection, the reign of the saints, and the final resurrection. They also do not authorize the completion of the chapter with chronological precision. Therefore, the study keeps these questions open and is limited to what the text and informed commentators actually affirm.
